title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Introduction
content: Despite the plethora of literature describing the traditional 12 pairs of cranial nerves, very little has been published on the seemingly innocuous nerve known as nervus terminalis, commonly referred to as the terminal nerve, nerve nulla (n), cranial nerve zero “0,” and cranial nerve XIII. However, this nerve has been identified in numerous invertebrate and vertebrate species, including humans, for more than a century. [1] Interestingly, this structure remains unrecognized mainly in the medical literature, particularly because most anatomy and medical textbooks have overlooked its existence, even though it has been identified in the human brain since 1914. Since then, a wide range of studies has described its embryology, histology, neurophysiology, and clinical significance.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Introduction
content: Studies of adult brains and fetuses have shown that the fibers of the vomeronasal organ and those of the olfactory nerve are independent of each other embryologically, as early as stages 17 and 18. In the late 1980s, it was named “cranial nerve 0” (CN0) for its position rostral to the official 12 cranial nerves. The CN0 neurons are associated with gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), suggesting a potential role in controlling human reproductive functions and behaviors. It has been speculated to play a role in the unconscious perception of specific odorants, influencing autonomic and reproductive hormonal systems via the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. [2] Furthermore, the literature suggests a potential role in detecting pheromones for mate selection and in neuromodulating reproductive functions. [3] [1]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Introduction
content: Researchers hypothesize that CN0 may trigger hormonal responses independently or with other neuroanatomical circuits, such as the kisspeptin neural network. In females, these cells are primarily localized in the preoptic area and the infundibular regions of the hypothalamus, representing a sexually dimorphic trait with potential clinical implications. Thus, the presence of CN0 is relevant to medicine from myriad clinical perspectives.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Structure and Function
content: The CN0 is located on the ventral surface of the human brain. Its plexiform fibers appear to run in proximity to CNI, the olfactory nerve. CN0 rests on the anterior surface of the brain in the region of the olfactory trigone and courses anteriorly on the medial surface of the olfactory tract and bulb. Medially, it forms a plexus of fibers closely associated with the olfactory stria (medial to the anterior perforated space), from where it enters the brain independently (see Image. Basal View of a Human Brain Dissection Depicting the Location of CN0 Plexiform Fibers Over the Medial Surface of Gyri Recti). Its structural composition consists of numerous smaller strands that branch and anastomose, elaborating an elongated plexus (plexiform). Its bilateral bundle of unmyelinated nerve fibers is most evident in human fetal stages. However, it is also seen in adult brains. [4]  Its fascicles can be seen within the subarachnoid space covering the gyri recti surface of the frontal lobe.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Structure and Function
content: In humans and a wide range of other species, the physiology of reproductive hormones is regulated by the HPG axis, and GnRH plays a pivotal role. The latter is released from the hypothalamus upon the appropriate neuronal induction. Once GnRH is released from hypothalamic neurons, it potentiates the synthesis and secretion of gonadotropins, specifically luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), from the adenohypophysis. This, in turn, regulates the production and secretion of the sex steroid hormones (eg, estrogens, testosterone) that ultimately command the sexual behaviors governing the biology of our reproduction. [2] The embryological migration pattern of GnRH cells and their direct association with CN0 suggest a potential role in the development of the human HPG axis. [5] Furthermore, it has been suggested that this nerve may have neuromodulatory effects via GnRH and the nasal mucosal blood vessels and glands, which could exert regulatory functions on human sexual behavior. [6] [7]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Embryology
content: Since the beginning of the 20th century, numerous studies have examined the embryological origins and developmental stages of human olfactory structures. [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] Although the embryological origin of the CN0 correlates with that of the rest of the human olfactory structures, the terminal nerve fibers appear to enter the brain along with the olfactory and vomeronasal nerve fibers at embryological stages 17 and 18. This is based on Bossy’s work (1980) and on preliminary studies detailing the Carnegie Collection from stages 11 to 23 of human embryos. [10] These have been pivotal in understanding the embryological development of the terminal nerve and other olfactory structures in human embryos. See Image. Further work by Muller et al provided reconstructions essential for understanding and interpreting the developmental processes of neural connections within and beyond olfactory system structures. [8]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Embryology
content: The specific embryological origin of CN0 remains somewhat enigmatic. While some authors have reported that the nerve originates in the olfactory placode, from which the olfactory cells also arise, others indicate that it arises from the neural crest. [13] [14] Perhaps it arises from the migration of cells from different embryonic lineages, among which the neural crest may contribute to the subset of GnRH-secreting neurons.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Physiologic Variants
content: Although CN0 is closely positioned next to the CNI (olfactory nerve), its functionality is distinct from the classical olfactory sensory role of perceiving odorant molecules via the olfactory receptors (ORs), which belong to a superfamily of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). [15] Various reports indicate that the terminal nerve projects to several important neuroanatomical structures, including the medial pre-commissural septum and the medial septal nucleus. It also sends fibers to the nasal mucosa and to rostral ventral brain structures, primarily olfactory and limbic areas (eg, the amygdala and hypothalamic nuclei). [16] [17] These connections provide access to the limbic system structures, such as the hypothalamus. In the hypothalamus, specifically within the preoptic (POA) and the infundibular (INF) nuclei, there is a relatively inconspicuous group of neurons collectively referred to as the "kisspeptin neuronal network". [18] This hypothalamic neuronal circuit is involved in the central endocrinologic control of puberty and human reproductive functions. The hypothalamic kisspeptin neuronal network primarily induces GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus, which, in turn, regulates gonadotropin secretion, including luteinizing hormone and FSH. These adenohypophyseal hormones ultimately influence the synthesis and secretion of sex steroids by the gonads. [19]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Physiologic Variants
content: The CN0's proposed neuromodulatory role in sexual behaviors via GnRH raises an interesting connection with hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons. While numerous elegant studies describe the efferent projections of the human kisspeptin neuronal network, its afferents remain poorly understood. [20] Perhaps the enigmatic CN0 is the missing link in this complex scientific conundrum. The CN0 has projections to the nasal mucosa, the amygdala, and the hypothalamus, among other structures. If, hypothetically, some of these projections reach the POA, INF, or both hypothalamic nuclei, they may represent a potential afferent component of the kisspeptin neurons that regulate GnRH secretion, thereby controlling human sexual behaviors and functions. Although exciting, this notion is merely speculative but warrants scientific investigation.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Physiologic Variants
content: Furthermore, during the last several decades, the idea of pheromones influencing human sexual behaviors has been a controversial topic. [21] [22] This naturally includes the even more controversial vomeronasal organ (VNO), a very discrete chemosensory organ located deep into the nasal cavity of vertebrates, including humans. [23] [24] [25] For many years, the VNO has been held responsible for intra-specific chemical communication via pheromones, which are chemical messengers secreted externally by an individual and detected by another of the same species. Many still debate the existence of the VNO and pheromones in humans. However, the evidence coming from many reputable studies is robustly supportive. [26] These studies suggest that humans possess genes for at least 6 pheromone receptor types, the same as those in mice. The presence of the VNO in humans has been extensively described in the literature. The VNO is present in human fetuses by weeks 6 to 7; its ducts have openings into the nasal cavity by the 28th week. Histologically, it consists of the olfactory epithelium, lamina propria, and a rich vascularization network. A recent Bulgarian study reported that the VNO is present in approximately 27% of adults (males, 53%; females, 47%). [27] Similar findings have been reported in other populations (eg, the United States, Canada, France, and Egypt).

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Physiologic Variants
content: Despite these important considerations, recent studies on the VNO suggest that this sexually dimorphic structure is vestigial in adult humans, namely a remnant of embryonic differentiation. This suggests that although present, this structure is not physiologically active in adulthood. Accordingly, the hypothesis linking the VNO to pheromone detection in adult humans lacks scientific support. Alternatively, a reasonable notion may implicate the nasal mucosa's nerve projections from CN0, transducing the inscrutable chemical signaling of adult human pheromones and regulating hypothalamic GnRH secretory pulses via the kisspeptin neuronal network, and consequently controlling gonadotropin and sex steroid secretion in response to pheromone chemical cues. However, this conceptual cascade of neuroendocrine events remains hypothetical, as the CN0 projections to hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons are speculative. Given that the VNO may lack physiological competence in adult pheromone detection, the CN0 may be a plausible candidate for this novel physiological role, independent of the VNO.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Surgical Considerations
content: The location of the CN0 fibers is in close relationship to the olfactory tract. Its nerve components converge into a dense plexus of fibers embedded within the dura mater, adjacent to the CNI and other nerve fibers. This may explain why CN0 fibers have consistently been mistaken for CNI in human dissections, imaging studies, and cranial surgical procedures. Furthermore, the CN0 fibers also travel through the minuscule foramina of the cribriform plate (ethmoid bone) towards the nasal cavity. The CN0 fibers then course on either side of the nasal septum and branch through the septal mucosa bilaterally. Herein, its fibers travel along the olfactory and nasopalatine nerve fibers.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Surgical Considerations
content: The anatomical positioning of CN0 poses important clinical considerations, especially for otorhinolaryngology surgical procedures. Given its potential neuroreproductive role, damage or laceration to CN0 during routine otolaryngological surgical procedures may compromise its structural integrity and function. In animal models, the laceration of the terminal nerve has been reported to cause GnRH deficiencies. However, there are no clinical studies to confirm these findings in humans.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Clinical Significance
content: In addition to the surgical considerations listed above, it is imperative to acknowledge the existence of CN0 and appreciate its potential medical relevance. For instance, Kallmann syndrome is an inherited condition associated with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (HH) and hyposmia or anosmia affecting both sexes. [28] Interestingly, an embryological failure in the normal migratory pattern of basal forebrain GnRH cells appears to be the primary cause of the hypogonadism associated with this human genetic condition. Studies have shown point mutations and deletions in KISS1R in some HH patients. [29] This suggests that the CN0 GnRH-containing axons play a pivotal role in the development and differentiation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. It may be potentially critical for the normal sexual development of both male and female patients.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Other Issues
content: One persistent argument regarding this nerve concerns its name. There has been some debate on how to refer to it properly in scientific terminology. While some argue it should remain the terminal nerve, given its location adjacent to the lamina terminalis, others have proposed alternative designations. Several suggestions have been made, including CN0, CN XIII, and others. [30] Since the nerve was discovered after the other CNs had been named and classified sequentially based on their anatomical location, some agree that CN XIII is most appropriate. CN XIII seems reasonable because the nerve was discovered last. However, this term appears counterintuitive, primarily because its anatomical location is rostral to all other cranial nerves. Accordingly, CN0 has been proposed as the most suitable, but some argued that it is discordant since zero "0" is not a Roman numeral. Therefore, it is inconsistent with the other CNs, which were enumerated using Roman numerals.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Other Issues
content: Aside from issues with anatomical nomenclature, CN0 can be an important topic in medical education. Not only is CN0 anatomically relevant given its long history in the scientific literature, but it is also clinically relevant for its role in normal and abnormal development and function, as illustrated by its potential involvement in Kallmann syndrome, which is commonly caused by mutations in the kisspeptin or GnRH signaling pathways. Embryologically, the development of CN0 occurs synchronously with the sensory structures of the olfactory system. Developmental disturbances in stages 17 and 18 have been linked to physiological abnormalities of the HPA axis, as described in Kallmann syndrome. Also, traumatic avulsion of the olfactory network plays a role in depression concomitant with anosmia in patients who experience sufficiently traumatic forces commonly associated with automobile collisions. Depression with anosmia has also been linked to symptoms such as reduced sexual drive and impaired recognition of emotion in others. [31]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 0 (Terminal Nerve) -- Other Issues
content: Medical and health sciences students benefit from a deeper understanding of the basic science and clinical aspects of traditional cranial nerve teaching, as well as the growing body of scientific evidence on CN0. Finally, CN0 is important in principle as a topic of ongoing scientific debates that shape the nature of the evidence-based practice that underpins medicine. Scientific knowledge evolves, resulting in changes to standards of practice and treatment options requiring medicine students to be "lifelong learners" for their patients' benefit.
